parts.title: Longer or better?
parts.brief: The problem the QALY solves: comparing treatments that add years with treatments that improve them, on one budget.
parts.figure: A comparison table that fills in row by row: columns 'Treatment', 'Longer life', 'Better life'. Row 1 'Cancer drug': longer yes, better no. Row 2 'Hip replacement': longer no, better yes. Row 3 'New treatment' (the running example): yes and yes. When years alone are counted, the 'Longer life' column is highlighted and the hip replacement's 'no' is underlined; when pain is counted instead, the 'Better life' column is highlighted and the cancer drug's 'no' is underlined. Finally the whole table is bracketed by one word: 'QALY' — one currency for both columns. Supporting piece: a small cue 'One budget' at the start — temporary, gone after line 3.
script: How do you compare a treatment that makes life longer with one that makes life better?
Every health service faces that question, because it has one budget and many treatments asking for it.
Take a cancer drug that gives patients extra months of life.
And a hip replacement, which adds no years, but takes away pain and brings back walking.
The natural first answer is to count the years of life each one adds.
By that count the hip replacement is worth nothing, which no one waiting for a new hip would accept.
Count pain or mobility instead, and the cancer drug's extra time vanishes from view.
Most treatments do some of both, like the new treatment in our running example for a 60-year-old with a chronic disease.
What we need is one currency that counts length and quality of life at once.
That currency is the quality-adjusted life year: the QALY.
Agencies such as NICE in England use it to decide which treatments public money pays for.
So the QALY exists to put very different treatments on one scale.

parts.title: The quality scale
parts.brief: The weight q: 1 is full health, 0 is dead, below 0 is worse than dead; the running example's two states placed on it.
parts.figure: A horizontal number line for the quality weight q, from -0.6 to 1 in steps of 0.2 (0.1 minor if possible). The end 1 is marked 'Full health', 0 is marked 'Dead'. The stretch between 0 and 1 is shaded 'Ill or limited'. A point at 0.5 labeled 'Standard care' appears, then a point at 0.7 labeled 'New treatment', with a hop arrow from 0.5 to 0.7 labeled '+0.2'. Last, the line's stretch below 0 is shaded 'Worse than dead' and a point near -0.59 is marked 'Worst EQ-5D state'. Supporting piece: a small cue 'q = quality weight' — temporary, gone after line 4.
script: Now that we want one currency, we need a scale for how good a year of life is.
Call it q, the quality weight of a health state; economists also call it a utility.
At one end, q equals 1: a year in full health.
At the other, q equals 0: dead.
Everything in between is a year lived with some illness or limitation.
Our patient on standard care sits at 0.5, so one year like that counts as half a year of full health.
On the new treatment, q rises to 0.7.
The scale does not stop at zero.
When people are asked, many rate the worst states, such as extreme pain with no ability to move or wash, as worse than being dead, so those get a weight below 0.
In the first UK value set for the EQ-5D questionnaire, the worst state scored about minus 0.59.
Where numbers like 0.5 and 0.7 come from is the next lecture's question; here, take them as given.
So q is an exchange rate: it says how many years of full health one year in that state is worth.

parts.title: Area under the line
parts.brief: QALYs as q times t, the area under the quality line: 2.0 on standard care, 3.5 on the new treatment, a gain of 1.5.
parts.figure: A QALY diagram with straight lines: time t in years (0 to 6) along the bottom, quality weight q (0 to 1) up the side. Standard care: flat at q = 0.5 from year 0 to year 4, then drops to 0; its area is shaded and labeled '2.0 QALYs'. Then standard care fades to a ghost, and the new treatment is drawn: flat at q = 0.7 from year 0 to year 5, then drops to 0; its area labeled '3.5 QALYs'. The area between the two paths is shaded as the gain, labeled 'ΔQ = 1.5'. Scratch card, one line as each is said: '4 × 0.5 = 2.0', '5 × 0.7 = 3.5', '3.5 − 2.0 = 1.5' — temporary, gone after line 10.
script: Now that each year has a weight, we can add up a whole stretch of life.
Time t runs along the bottom, in years, and the weight q runs up the side.
On standard care, our patient lives four years at q equals 0.5.
The QALYs are the area under that line: 4 times 0.5, which is 2.0 QALYs.
So four years at half quality count the same as two years in full health.
Now the new treatment, for the same patient with the same disease.
Five years at q equals 0.7: 5 times 0.7, which is 3.5 QALYs.
Part of the gain is the extra year; part is that every year is better.
The difference, which we call delta Q, is 1.5 QALYs.
Counting years alone would have said one year gained, blind to the better quality.
Real quality lines are rarely flat, but the rule is the same: add up q times t, the area under the line.
So a QALY is simply area: how long, times how well.

parts.title: Where the idea came from
parts.brief: A short history from Klarman's kidney study to the name and to NICE, then the synthesis: one yardstick for length and quality.
parts.figure: A horizontal timeline, milestones appearing one per line: '1968 Klarman' (sublabel 'kidney care'), '1970 Fanshel & Bush' (sublabel 'health index'), '1976 Zeckhauser & Shepard' (sublabel 'the name', emphasized), '1985 Williams' (sublabel 'bypass surgery'), '1999 NICE' (sublabel 'cost per QALY'). At the synthesis the running example returns as a small readout '2.0 → 3.5 QALYs' — temporary, shown from line 9 to the end. Quiz: A treatment adds no years, but lifts q from 0.5 to 0.7 over the patient's 4 remaining years. How many QALYs does it gain? | 0 | 0.2 | 0.8 | 2.8 | correct: 3 | wrong hint: The gain in each year is the change in q; now count how many years get it.
script: Now that we can compute a QALY, where did the idea come from?
In 1968, Herbert Klarman and colleagues compared kidney dialysis with transplants, and counted a year with a working transplant as worth more than a year on dialysis.
That was the core move: adjust years of life for their quality.
In 1970, Fanshel and Bush built a health status index to put such weights on one scale.
In 1976, Richard Zeckhauser and Donald Shepard gave the idea its name: the quality-adjusted life year.
In 1985, Alan Williams at York used QALYs to weigh heart bypass surgery against other uses of the same money.
In 1999, England set up NICE, which came to judge new treatments by their cost per QALY.
Today health technology assessment agencies in many countries do the same.
Back to our 60-year-old: 2.0 QALYs on standard care, 3.5 on the new treatment.
Because length and quality now share one unit, that gain can stand beside a cancer drug or a new hip.
That is what the QALY gives us: one yardstick for very different kinds of health.
Whether the yardstick is fair, and whether it measures what matters, is what the rest of this course argues about.
